689.t: Hearing Joe Oliver in New Orleans: picnics, wind and the break
689.s: Oliver drew away Dominique's picnic crowd at the lake pavilions, had long wind, and his blues break snagged Louis and Dominique.
689.q: Yeah, well, somewhere he died. Savannah, Georgia. But Joe's a good musician. He played a few parades with many parades. The same King Oliver.

568.t: Joe Oliver and the rivalry of the dozens
568.s: Oliver worked the next corner, and the two traded insults and played the dozens.
568.q: Oh yeah. Yeah, because Mr. Groeschel, he was determined because I'm working at one corner, and he's at Pete Lawless at the next corner. See? And Joe, they'd all pass and kick one another at night. If he'd see my boss out there, he'd tell him, say, you better get a band in there, I'd say, cut that…

2.t: Joe Oliver's big tone, mutes, and Johnny Dodds's theory of the band breakup
2.s: They note Oliver's tone can't be judged from records; Russell recalls Mutt Carey on mutes and Johnny Dodds's tone theory for why Oliver's band broke up.
2.q: No, that's right. On the records, you can't tell how big his tone was. But from all the evidence, about 100% of it, you might say, of anybody that ever talked about him in the old days that heard him, talk about the big tone. That he was almost like, say, a second Bolden after Bolden, that he had…

288.t: Learning your audience; King Oliver in the Irish Channel
288.s: Charles says his smooth style failed with rough Italian crowds who wanted Oliver's growling mute work.
288.ch: Maple Leaf, own orchestra and rivals
288.q: You see, old King Oliver, he'd take one number there, you'd be playing that whole number almost, and he'd be just right there. Peep, peepireep, you see? That's all he'd be doing. And they liked that. But I couldn't see that.

8.t: Sending for Joe Oliver and his first night at the Royal Garden
8.s: Garland was in Chicago before Oliver and sent for him when the Royal Garden opened; Oliver went over big using mutes.
8.q: no when he first came you see I was playing with they used to play with him in New Orleans you see he played with us with Oliver but when after I got up there Wages Williams wanted to open up the up the the this the Royal Garden and I sent for Joe for him off to play for him yeah I see then after…

24.t: Joe Oliver's brick and his pistol at rehearsal
24.s: Allen relays a story of Oliver using a brick to cue the band; Moore describes Oliver bringing a pistol to rehearsals while Dave Nelson ran them. A tape restart follows.
24.ch: Jelly Roll Morton and Oliver anecdotes
24.q: Well, he didn't exactly mean what he was doing, but that's his way. When he come called rehearsal, he bring his gun with him, you know? Great gun about that long.

715.t: Hearing Oliver and Armstrong; comparison of styles
715.s: He heard Oliver and Armstrong in St. Louis, later played with Oliver in New York, and discusses whether his style resembled Oliver's.
715.q: Yeah. He was only about two years younger than I. I was born in December. He was about three years old. Three years at the most. Did you get to hear Oliver play in those years? Yeah, I used to marry Oliver and Louis Armstrong because when they came up to San Luis, that's before I worked on them…

23.t: King Oliver's 1923 Chicago band and the two-cornet breaks
23.s: Rose says the 1923 band fit the form only some of the time. Two cornets were unusual indoors in New Orleans, and Oliver signalled Louis Armstrong's breaks by fingering the valves.
23.ch: New Orleans bands, Oliver and Armstrong
23.q: I would say that it, that it frequently fits the description, but not, not all the time. Uh, by the time you had Oliver in New Orleans, in Chicago, uh, you already had a set band for one thing, which had the opportunity to play a location job for a long period of time. Mm-hmm. And to, uh, to some…

639.t: Joe Oliver compared with Louis Armstrong
639.s: He describes Oliver's dirty tone and mute use, how Louis learned from him, and anecdotes about Oliver's eye and derby.
639.ch: Joe Oliver, Tom Brown and closing
639.q: Yeah, I think, well of course Louie doesn't have much resemblance to Joe Oliver anymore, although I think he's, uh, contrary to most, uh, died in the world jazz people, I think he's a very great performer, jazz performer today. He just hasn't been in good settings. But Joe Oliver had a dirty tone,…

77.t: King Oliver, the soft-playing one-eyed trumpeter
77.s: Oliver was big, had one eye, and could play so softly it could not be heard across the room; he and Louis together made beautiful music.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: Oh, he was fine. He was a great big man, not what you'd call fat, but big, tall and healthy looking, you know. And he had one eye. He had one eye.
